points.requirement: A marker-outcome association among people differs from agreement between randomized treatment effects on marker and clinical outcome across trials. Grouping achieved responders does not preserve randomized treatment assignment.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A surrogate is a measured outcome used in place of a direct clinical-benefit outcome, with evidence needed for that substitution in the intended setting. Two relationships must be separated: people with a favourable marker may have better outcomes, while treatments that improve that marker may or may not improve the outcome. The first is a prognostic association; the second concerns agreement between treatment effects across suitable randomised comparisons. A treatment can change another pathway, later disease or toxicity as well as the marker. Validation is specific to disease, treatment context and intended outcome. An early measure is not automatically validated, and regulatory acceptance in one programme does not transfer to another. “Validated” and “reasonably likely to predict benefit” carry different evidence claims. Even a pathology or imaging response does not capture every benefit and harm.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A fictional two-level example separates people from trials. In the patient panel, all 20 people have complete follow-up to year 3: 10 achieved a pathological complete response and 10 did not. Two of the first 10 and six of the second 10 have an event by year 3.
